title: Is Your CV Getting Rejected? 5 Mistakes You Must Fix
description:
The CV Mistakes That Get You Rejected in Seconds | 5 Fixes to Get Interviews


Recruiters spend about 7 seconds scanning your CV before they decide to bin it or keep reading, and most CVs get rejected on the same handful of mistakes. This video breaks down the 5 CV mistakes that get you rejected in seconds, and the exact fixes that get you interviews, from someone who built the recruitment software hiring teams use to filter candidates.

If you're sending applications and hearing nothing back, your CV is almost certainly making at least one of these 5 mistakes. Fix them and you'll get more out of your CV than another 100 applications ever would.


What you'll learn in this video:
- Why a human, not the ATS, rejects your CV in the first 7 seconds
- The what, how, why formula that turns weak bullet points into results, with real before and after examples
- Why a profile summary is wasting the most valuable space on your CV if you have under 10 years of experience
- The skills section and certification mistakes quietly lowering your interview rate
- How to tailor 1 strong CV per role and get interviews at more than double the rate, 4.23% vs 2.07%, from a study of 39,000 CVs


VIDEO CHAPTERS:
0:00 Why your CV gets rejected in 7 seconds
0:41 Mistake 1, bullet points with no results
1:00 The what, how, why bullet formula
3:02 Mistake 2, the profile summary killing your top third
4:22 Mistake 3, a skills section full of fluff
5:56 Mistake 4, the template that breaks the scan
7:01 Mistake 5, the same CV sent everywhere
7:25 Why tailoring doubles your interview rate
7:49 Your 5 fixes for this week
8:12 Find what's actually killing your CV


If you want to know exactly which of these is holding your CV back, here's where to start:

FREE DIAGNOSIS:
Take the free 2-minute diagnosis. Get your personalised employability score plus a roadmap of exactly what to fix first in your job search.
https://the.offeraccelerator.uk/new-candidate-diagnosis?source=youtube&utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=description&utm_campaign=cv-mistakes-rejected-in-seconds


CONNECT WITH ME
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/olivercordingley
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/olivercordingley


WATCH NEXT:
ATS Isn't Rejecting Your CV. This Is. (3 Real Filters)


ABOUT ME:
I dropped out of university at 19 to build recruitment software and ATS systems used by hiring teams. For years I spoke to hundreds of hiring managers and recruiters every day, learning exactly how candidates get filtered, shortlisted, and hired from the inside. I started coaching friends through their job search using what I'd seen, then raised investment, built a software company, and hired my own team. I've seen hiring from every angle.

Today I help job seekers land offers faster using a proven 3-step system. I've coached hundreds of candidates into roles at firms like JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, EY, and PwC and many more.

transcript: The reason your CV keeps getting rejected in seconds has almost nothing to do with the ATS and everything to do with one thing a human looks for in that first seven seconds and that's results. These are actual numbers that prove you were good at the job that you're applying for. So if your bullet points are just a list of, you know, things that you were responsible for, you're getting binned before they even read your second line. Now I had someone that I coached send me their CV last month. They paid an agency three figures for a professional rewrite and they were still getting rejected everywhere. And sure, their new CV, it looked great, but not a single bullet point on it had a result that actually related to the job. So we fixed exactly that. We changed nothing else about the experience and they were getting interviews within two weeks. So that's mistake number one of five and that's the biggest. It's the bullet points with no results. The other four are the wasted profile summary sat at the top, a skill section full of stuff that nobody can check, a template that breaks the way recruiters read and one generic CV you fire at everything. So let me show you how to fix all five starting with those bullet points. So the fix here is the same structure every single time. Every bullet point on your CV should say what you did with a strong verb, how you did it with actual tools or skills and what came out of it, ideally a number. So instead of writing responsible for managing the team budget, you would write led a quarterly budget review using Excel and found 12% in annual savings that got reinvested into a new product. It's the same job, just a completely different signal to people looking at your CV. For example, instead of handled customer queries, you would write resolved over 200 customer queries a week using Zendesk and cut the average response time from 24 hours to under six. And another one, instead of worked on the marketing team, you can write six email campaigns that brought 1200 leads and lifted pipeline by 33%. So one version is going to get skimmed, you know, straight past and the other is what stops people. It catches their eye because it's got action, it's got a method, and the result. And a quick bit of context on why I know this actually matters. So, I dropped out of university to build recruitment software, and the actual systems that recruiters and hiring managers use to screen candidates. And I spent years talking to hundreds of hiring managers, watching how they actually read CVs. So, this isn't theory, it's exactly what is happening on the other side of your application. And one thing that people get wrong when they hear this is that they go to cram numbers into everything. You don't need five numbers in a bullet point. You need one, maybe two, that actually means something. So, be honest about the verbs as well. Like, if you write led a team, make sure you actually led them. You didn't just sit near them. Because led, for example, means that you made them better, whereas managed just means that you existed above them on an org chart. Now, if you genuinely can't put a number on something, then describe the change instead. So, something like, "Built the onboarding checklist that became a standard process for the whole team." What you'd never do is fall back on responsible for or involved in, a bullet that says contributed to various projects is honestly worse than no bullet point at all. So, mistake number two is a profile summary sat right at the top of your CV. And to understand why that's a problem, you need to know how recruiters and hiring managers actually read your CV. So, their eyes, when they're scanning your CV, move in a capital F shape. So, it's across the top first, and then down the left-hand side, and then they're basically done. So, the top third of your CV is the single most valuable space on the entire page. And most people fill it with four lines of generic stuff like, "I'm hard-working, detail-oriented professional with strong communication skills and a passion for X, like, whatever." Nobody reads that section, and it's true probably of most of the candidates applying for that job. So, it doesn't signal anything, and then worse, it's actually shoving your actual valuable experience down the page where it barely gets looked at. So, if you've got less than 10 years of experience, cut the summary completely, and let your best, most relevant role sit in that top third instead. Because that role with impressive results on it is far better opening than just a paragraph about how driven you are. And then back to that 10-year experience less or more than point, like that's not arbitrary, there's a reason behind it. So, there's research on over 39,000 CVs showing that the people earlier in their career, a summary has basically zero impact. And sometimes you can actually negatively impact your interview rates. So, the only time that summary earns its space is if you're genuinely senior or you're changing careers and you need a one or two-line summary to bridge your story. So, mistake number three is that a skill section that's just stuffed and crammed with just keywords and random stuff they can't check, like communication, leadership, teamwork, or even hard skills where you haven't mentioned it in the experience. Cuz every candidate on the planet list these and none of them mean anything on their own because you can't prove them in a list or in context. So, strip your skill section back to the absolute core major ones. Those the programming languages, the software tools, the methodology, spoken languages, real certifications that have value. And only put stuff in there that you actually can prove in context in your experiences as well. So, for example, if you're a finance analyst, you'd put something like Excel, Bloomberg, and SQL. For a marketer, it'd be something like Google Analytics, HubSpot, SEMrush. And to do one better, your skills, they don't belong in a list. You need to prove them in your experience bullets where the results do the actual talking. So, for example, just listing SQL in your skill section doesn't count for much on its own. And it lands much harder when it shows up inside a bullet in context doing something. So, for example, "Analyze 50,000 rows on customer data in SQL to find where they were losing sign-ups." That's a massive difference between just claiming a skill in a list and then actually proving it in context. And one more thing on the certifications as well, before I forget, is that most people get this bit wrong. More certifications is not better. That same research on the 39,000 CVs found that once you list more than about eight certifications, your interview rate actually drops because the recruiter or the hiring manager, they can't find the one that they actually care about. So, pick one or two maximum that actually matter for the role and then cut the rest. So, mistake number four is the template itself and this one catches people who think they're being clever. You download a fancy CV builder template with two columns and a colored sidebar and a little skills bar chart, maybe a photo, whatever and it looks designed and it looks great, but it's quietly killing you. There is no ATS system that rewards a template. Full stop. So, do not CV templates that promise it's ATS friendly or optimized because the ATS does not look at the layout, it looks at the words. Now, where a template is important is that human read which decides if you get into the interview or not. So, that two-column structure for example, that will confuse the natural human scanning technique of that F shape that I spoke about earlier. And again, if you're starting adding graphics and sidebars, that just gets in the way of the stuff that actually matters. So, go into your CV, make it as plain, clean, and simple as possible. Use simple fonts and just put your name at the top in bigger letters and then everything else is the same size. And if anything doesn't fit at all, cut the content. Don't shrink the font down to eight point because if they can't read it, they won't read it. And mistake number five is actually tailoring your CV for every single job because when you do that, you're probably ending up using ChatGPT and you're just sounding like everybody else in the pile. And just reading like everybody else is exactly how you would get ignored. Now, I'm not telling you to build 20 different CVs. That's a trap and it eats your hours and it usually makes things worse. The reason people get told to tailor endlessly is that they're applying to five completely different job titles at once and then of course, nothing is going to land. So, what you need to do instead is pick one target and have one strong CV for that target role. And then from time to time, if the job description slightly changes, you can then make subtle tweaks to that one CV. But remember, one job title, one CV, and that should be your entire job search. So, those are the five mistakes. So, get the results into your bullet points, cut the summary if you're earlier in your career, keep your skills section to hard skills only, and go to that single column with a clean template, and just position one strong CV with one role instead of trying to blast it everywhere, constantly trying to tailor it. So, make sure you fix those five things this week, and you'll get more out of your CV than another 100 applications ever would. Now, if you're watching this and thinking you're still not sure what is killing your chances and what is wrong with your CV, I've built a free 2-minute diagnosis that exactly tells you. So, what you need to do is answer a few questions about where you're at, and it gives you a personalized score plus a road map of exactly what to fix first, whether that's your CV, your LinkedIn, or the way you're applying. Now, it's completely free, and the link is in the description, so go and take it. And I will personally review your CV and LinkedIn as well. And also, if you want to learn how the ATS actually works and how it's not rejecting you despite what half the internet keeps telling you, you need to watch this one next because I'll show you exactly what is actually filtering your CV before a human ever sees it.
